title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
description: Brute force to optimized: a linear scan versus a modified binary search that identifies the genuinely sorted half at every midpoint.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a sorted array of distinct integers that has been rotated at an unknown pivot, and a target value, return the index of target if it exists in the array, or -1 if not, in O(log n) time.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Even though the array is rotated, at any midpoint, AT LEAST ONE of the two halves [lo, mid] or [mid, hi] is still fully sorted (the rotation point can only be in one of them). Recognizing which half is sorted, and whether target falls within its range, lets binary search proceed despite the rotation.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Deck of Cards Cut and Restacked
blocks.text: Picture a sorted deck of cards that has been cut at some point and the two halves swapped (the bottom half placed on top). Looking at any middle card, one side of it is still guaranteed to be in perfect ascending order, even though the deck as a whole is not; you can use that sorted side to decide where to look next.

blocks.caption: At every midpoint, one half is always fully sorted; check if target falls within that half's range

blocks.text: Result: index 4. The array is sorted [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] rotated to start at index 4.

Before treating the rotation as an obstacle to binary search, notice that at any midpoint, comparing nums[lo] to nums[mid] reveals which half is genuinely sorted, and checking whether target falls within that sorted half's value range tells you definitively whether to search there or the other half.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left half [lo, mid] is fully sorted (no rotation point within it).

Observation 2: In that case, if target lies within [nums[lo], nums[mid]), it must be in the sorted left half, so search there; otherwise, it must be in the right half (which contains the rotation point).

Observation 3: Symmetrically, if nums[lo] > nums[mid], the right half [mid, hi] is fully sorted instead, and the same range-check logic applies in reverse.

Observation 4: Regardless of which half is sorted, exactly one comparison (checking target against the sorted half's bounds) is enough to decide which half to keep searching, preserving O(log n) overall.

This leads to a modified binary search: at each midpoint, determine which half is sorted (by comparing nums[lo] to nums[mid]), check if target falls within that sorted half's range, and narrow the search accordingly.
Scan the array from left to right, comparing each element to target directly, ignoring the sorted (rotated) structure entirely.

items: Iterate over every index i from 0 to n-1.
If nums[i] equals target, return i.
If the loop completes without a match, return -1.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A linear scan works regardless of rotation, correct but ignoring the array's underlying sorted structure entirely.
This costs O(n), even though the rotated-sorted structure allows O(log n).

blocks.text: Limitation: the rotated array still has a genuinely sorted half at every midpoint; exploiting this via a modified binary search achieves O(log n).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why plain binary search does not directly apply: the rotation means nums[mid] is not simply "greater or less than everything on one side," so a naive comparison to target alone is insufficient.

The key structural fact: at any midpoint, exactly one of [lo, mid] or [mid, hi] is guaranteed to be a genuinely sorted (non-rotated) subarray, since the single rotation point can only fall within one of them.

Deciding which half to search: first identify which half is sorted (compare nums[lo] to nums[mid]); then check whether target's value falls within that sorted half's range; if so, search there, otherwise search the other (rotated) half.

The core idea: a modified binary search that first identifies the sorted half at each step, then uses a range check to decide where target could be.
At each midpoint, determine whether the left half or right half is sorted. Check if target falls within the sorted half's value range; if so, narrow to that half, otherwise narrow to the other half.

blocks.caption: Identify the sorted half at each midpoint, then check if target falls within its range

blocks.text: At every midpoint, comparing nums[lo] to nums[mid] correctly identifies which half is genuinely sorted, since the rotation point can only exist in one of the two halves. Once the sorted half is known, checking whether target falls within its value range definitively determines whether target could be there (search that half) or must be in the other, rotated half (search there instead), preserving the O(log n) halving behavior of standard binary search despite the rotation.

blocks.text: Search in Rotated Sorted Array is the canonical "modified binary search" problem, showing that binary search still applies even when the array is not fully sorted, as long as SOME exploitable structure (a sorted half) remains at every step.

items: Using strict inequalities incorrectly in the range checks, mishandling the boundary values nums[lo] or nums[hi] themselves.
Forgetting the "<=" in nums[lo] <= nums[mid], which matters when the search range has shrunk to a single or two-element span.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "one half is always sorted, so identify it and check if target falls in its range" is the key insight to state clearly before coding.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "sorted array but rotated at an unknown point", think: at every midpoint, one half is genuinely sorted, use a range check on that half to decide where to search.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The linear scan runs in O(n) time; the modified binary search runs in O(log n) time, both using O(1) space.

items: Pattern: modified binary search, identifying the genuinely sorted half at each midpoint despite the rotation.
Core Idea: compare nums[lo] to nums[mid] to find the sorted half; check if target falls within that half's range to decide where to search.
Time: O(n) for the linear scan, O(log n) for the modified binary search.
Most Important Observation: at every midpoint of a rotated sorted array, at least one half is still genuinely sorted.
Interview Difficulty: a very well-known, frequently asked modified binary search problem.
One line memory trick: find the sorted half, check if target is in its range, search accordingly.
